neighbours.label: marking that only one option or explanation is possible: 'can only', 'no other', 'no alternative', 'nowhere else'
fire: After the bridge collapsed, the villagers had no other way to reach the town.
Such a sudden drop in sales can only be explained by the new competitor.
Once the dam was built, the fish had nowhere else to spawn.
With the budget frozen, the school had no alternative but to close the library.
The fingerprints on the glass could only have come from the gardener.
Stranded in the storm, the hikers saw no other option than to wait.
This kind of damage can only be caused by a very strong earthquake.
When the shop closed, the elderly residents had nowhere else to buy bread.
quiet: After the bridge was repaired, the villagers had a quicker way to reach the town.
Such a sudden drop in sales might be explained by several different factors.
Once the dam was built, the fish moved upstream to spawn in spring.
With the budget increased, the school decided to expand the library.
The fingerprints on the glass were sent to the lab for analysis.
Stranded in the storm, the hikers checked their maps and waited.
The museum has only three paintings by this artist in its collection.
When the shop reopened, the elderly residents bought bread there every day.

predictions: fire items 0.4-0.75 at only/other/else/alternative; near misses with the option left open, or 'only' as a plain quantity restrictor, below 0.1
notes: Probe: 'nowhere else to go' 0.734, 'no alternative but' 0.617, 'no other choice than' 0.544, 'can only be described as' 0.520, 'could only have been achieved' 0.450; 'can be described as a partial success' 0.031, 'a good choice of buyers' 0.014, sentence-initial 'Only three students' 0.013. Near misses include mid-sentence quantity 'only' to test the distinction (not probed mid-sentence).
